name: Medium
tagline: A hosted blogging platform with a paywalled reader membership and a recommendation feed that decides who sees your work.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The writing surface is the easy part: a markdown editor, a static site generator and a clean reading theme is genuinely a one-shot build, and it will look better than Medium because you control the typography. What you cannot build is the reason most people publish there, which is other people's attention. Medium is a distribution machine with a membership pool that pays writers based on read time, plus an existing readership that arrives without you doing anything. A self-hosted blog starts with zero readers and stays that way until you do the marketing Medium was doing for you. Build the blog anyway if you already have an audience elsewhere, but do it knowing you are replacing a distribution channel with an empty room.
coreLoopDIY: Write markdown files locally, run a build, and get a fast static blog with RSS, tags and clean reading typography deployed anywhere.
requirements: A domain and any static host
Willingness to write markdown instead of using a WYSIWYG editor
whatYouLose: The recommendation feed and the readers it sends you for free
Member earnings based on read time from the paywall pool
Built-in follower graph, claps, highlights and comments
Publications, which are the closest thing Medium has to editorial distribution
A mobile app people already have installed
moatNotes: The paywall pool is the interesting bit: readers pay Medium, Medium pays writers, and neither side can be replicated by one person with a static site generator.
whyPeopleStillPay: Readers pay because a five dollar membership is a cheap way to unlock a large pile of decent writing without hunting for it, and the feed does the hunting. Writers stay because publishing somewhere with existing traffic beats publishing somewhere with none, especially if they do not want to think about hosting, SEO, email lists or design. The honest trade is that you rent the audience and Medium keeps the relationship, which is fine right up until it changes the algorithm.
notes: The blog is an afternoon; the readers are not. The moat is a paywalled membership pool plus a recommendation feed that hands writers an audience they did not earn.
prompt:
Build a static personal publishing site: a self-hosted blog with Medium-quality reading typography.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Astro with TypeScript, content collections for posts
- Markdown/MDX files in src/content/posts
- Plain CSS, no Tailwind, no UI framework
- Zero client-side JS except a tiny theme toggle

In scope:
- Post frontmatter: title, subtitle, publishDate, tags[], draft, coverImage, canonicalUrl
- Home page: reverse-chronological list with title, subtitle, date, read time estimate
- Post page: max 68ch measure, serif body at 20px/1.7, generous margins, styled blockquotes, code blocks with syntax highlighting, figure captions, footnotes
- Reading time computed from word count at build time
- Tag index pages at /tags and /tags/[tag]
- RSS feed at /rss.xml and a sitemap
- Open Graph tags per post, with a fallback image
- Draft posts excluded from all builds when draft: true
- Dark mode via prefers-color-scheme plus a manual toggle stored in localStorage
- A /now and /about page from markdown
- One npm script: npm run new -- "Post title" that scaffolds a dated markdown file with frontmatter filled in
- Ship three example posts covering headings, images, code, lists and a long quote so the typography is visible

Out of scope, do not build:
- Accounts, comments, claps, follows, analytics, telemetry, newsletters, payments
- A WYSIWYG editor. Markdown files are the interface.
- Any external API. The build must work fully offline.

Requirements:
- No secrets needed. If you add any config, use .env and commit .env.example only.
- README with: how to write a post, how to preview, how to deploy the static output to any host, and how to point a custom domain at it.
- Run the build and fix everything until npm run build passes clean with zero warnings.
